analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuels a rising per-ton emissions fee and sends quarterly rebates to most adults.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors in September 2024, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and received no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a fee on oil, gas, and coal based on their carbon emissions, starting at $65 per ton in 2026 and rising each year, with faster increases if emissions fail to fall on schedule. Most of the money would be returned to adults as quarterly tax-free payments, phased out for higher incomes, with the rest funding a new government bank for clean energy projects and grants for communities and workers hurt by the shift away from fossil fuels. It also includes border charges on imports and refunds for exports so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut by countries without carbon fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults with income under $75,000 (or $150,000 for joint filers) receive the full quarterly rebate, tax-free and not counted as income for other benefits, so most lower- and middle-income households would come out ahead even after the fee raises fuel prices. Communities overburdened by industrial pollution are guaranteed at least 40% of the grant funds, and workers and regions that depend on coal, oil, and gas get retraining, cleanup, and transition grants. Farmers get payments for adopting practices that reduce emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Lower- and middle-income adults, polluted communities, energy workers

how_it_helps.text: Each eligible adult receives quarterly rebate payments from the fund, with full payments for households earning under $75,000 single or $150,000 joint, phased out above that, and payments are tax-free and excluded from income for federal benefit eligibility [S2].

The bill requires that at least 40% of annual grant funds go to communities disproportionately harmed by pollution and climate impacts, including low-income, rural, Tribal, and communities of color [S2].

Workers and communities that rely on carbon-intensive industries get transition grants for job training, apprenticeships, early-retirement subsidies, cleanup of coal ash, mines, and abandoned wells, with construction paid Davis-Bacon prevailing wages and made with U.S.-made iron, steel, and manufactured goods [S2].

The fee is designed to fall on large emitters — refineries, coal producers, natural gas producers, importers, and industrial sources above 25,000 tons a year — with refunds for carbon capture and border adjustments so imports face equivalent charges and exporters are reimbursed [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, and importers pay the fee on their products, and large industrial facilities pay on their process emissions; the cost shows up in fuel and product prices. Higher-income households above the rebate phaseout absorb the fee without full offsets, and households that burn unusually large amounts of fuel — long commutes, fuel-oil heat, heavy trucking — may pay more than they get back. Treasury also puts up large initial appropriations before fee money arrives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy fossil fuel users

drawbacks.text: The fee raises energy prices immediately while rebates only begin later, and households above the phaseout or with high fuel use — long commutes, fuel-oil heating, small trucking businesses — could pay more than they receive back [S2].

The bill appropriates about $100 billion up front ($7.5 billion plus $37.5 billion plus $5 billion in each of fiscal 2025 and 2026) before carbon fee revenue exists, adding to federal borrowing in the near term [S2].

It creates a new independent federal lending corporation with a seven-member board and broad discretion over grants and loan guarantees, a structure critics of green banks argue adds bureaucracy and lends to projects the bill itself says are too risky for private capital [S2].

A good-faith objection: the fee path is fixed in statute ($65 plus $10 a year, inflation-adjusted) rather than set by regulators, so it could be either too rigid to adjust to economic conditions or too generous to stop rising if a future Congress wanted to cap it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most lower- and middle-income households the rebate is designed to exceed the price increases from the fee, which makes this a progressive design rather than a regressive energy tax. The serious costs fall on fossil fuel producers and on the minority of households that use a lot of fuel without qualifying for the full rebate, plus near-term federal borrowing of about $100 billion. Whether the climate benefit is worth the disruption depends on how fast the fee actually changes energy choices; the bill hard-codes targets of 45% emissions reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050 and accelerates the fee if targets are missed. It is a large, consequential redesign of energy taxation, not a narrow tweak, and its main design risk is the transition shock between prices rising and rebates arriving.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Durbin introduced it and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin of Illinois introduced the bill on September 19, 2024, less than four months before the end of the 118th Congress [S1][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; no further action is recorded [S4].
No member of either party cosponsored the bill [S3].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any hearing in the Senate, and expired when the Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and energy-intensive manufacturers are better off because the carbon fee never advanced, and no senator had to take a recorded position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Sen. Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no markup, hearing, or vote — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred; the bill's only Senate sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so it never reached the point of a partisan split.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers and refiners
industries.note: Covered entities — refinery operators, coal producers, natural gas producers, and importers — would owe the fee on every ton of greenhouse gas content of their fuels, starting at $65 in 2026 and rising $10 a year, with a parallel fee on their methane and process emissions from 2028 onward. The bill never advanced, so the industry avoided the charge entirely.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: They would pay fees on process emissions and on fossil fuel inputs, but the bill refunds fees on exported products and imposes equivalent charges on imports, protecting them from competitors in countries without carbon fees. Their bottom-line exposure would depend heavily on how regulators set the equivalency fees.

industries.industry: Clean energy and green bank sector
industries.note: A new Climate Change Finance Corporation would provide grants and 75% loan guarantees for solar, wind, storage, geothermal, EV charging, and industrial decarbonization projects, with priority for overburdened communities and Davis-Bacon wages. Clean energy builders and lenders would gain a large new source of project finance.

Farmers and ranchers would receive transition payments for adopting verifiable climate-smart practices that reduce emissions, with priority for underserved producers. Producers in violation of air or water rules would be barred from payments.

Eligible lenders including banks, credit unions, and community development financial institutions would originate loans backed by 75% federal guarantees and collect capped guarantee fees, expanding their clean energy lending business.
